definitions.explanation: A class of supernatural beings, spirits, and monsters from Japanese folklore. Yokai range from malevolent demons to mischievous tricksters to benign spirits, and include creatures like kappa, tengu, tanuki, and oni. A central concept in Japanese mythology and popular culture.

examples.japanese: {日本|にほん}には{様々|さまざま}な{妖怪|ようかい}の{伝説|でんせつ}がある。
examples.english: Japan has legends about various yokai.

examples.japanese: {子供|こども}のころ、{妖怪|ようかい}の{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いて{怖|こわ}がった。
examples.english: As a child, I was scared hearing stories about yokai.

examples.japanese: {妖怪|ようかい}を{題材|だいざい}にしたアニメや{漫画|まんが}は{日本|にほん}だけでなく{海外|かいがい}でも{人気|にんき}がある。
examples.english: Anime and manga featuring yokai are popular not only in Japan but also overseas.

notes:
COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {妖怪|ようかい}{伝説|でんせつ}: yokai legends
- {妖怪|ようかい}{退治|たいじ}: yokai slaying
- {妖怪|ようかい}{図鑑|ずかん}: yokai encyclopedia/guide
- {妖怪|ようかい}の{正体|しょうたい}: the true identity of a yokai

CULTURAL NOTE:
{妖怪|ようかい} are deeply rooted in Japanese culture and appear extensively in literature, art, anime, manga, and games. Famous examples include {河童|かっぱ} (kappa, water creature), {天狗|てんぐ} (tengu, long-nosed mountain spirit), {鬼|おに} (oni, ogre/demon), and {狐|きつね} (fox spirit). The painter {鳥山石燕|とりやませきえん} (Toriyama Sekien) catalogued many yokai in the Edo period, and modern works like {水木|みずき}しげるの「ゲゲゲの{鬼太郎|きたろう}」have kept yokai in popular consciousness.

SIMILAR WORDS:
{妖怪|ようかい} vs {幽霊|ゆうれい}: {幽霊|ゆうれい} specifically refers to ghosts (spirits of the dead). {妖怪|ようかい} is a broader category encompassing all manner of supernatural creatures, not limited to the dead.

{妖怪|ようかい} vs {化|ば}け{物|もの}: {化|ば}け{物|もの} (monster) is a more colloquial term that can include yokai but also refers to anything monstrous or abnormally large.
